newsitem.title: UK: NATO moves into top gear on Russia, enlargement.
newsitem.headline: NATO moves into top gear on Russia, enlargement.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
NATO, given a resolute push by the United States, forged ahead on Wednesday with efforts to convince Russia that it has nothing to fear from the alliance's expansion into Central and Eastern Europe.

But Moscow showed no sign of easing its bitter opposition to the enlargement of its Cold War foe, pushing instead for more concessions and saying the NATO plan showed blatant disregard for Russian concerns.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on her first foreign trip since taking up the job, held talks in London after discussions with NATO allies in Brussels on Tuesday.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel visited Moscow, the latest in a stream of top Western politicians who are trying to soothe Russian fears and wounded pride over the success of its Cold War foe. Kinkel appeared to make little progress.
Albright also travels to Moscow this week with a message she made clear in Brussels -- that Russian opposition to the alliance's enlargement will not deflect it from its course.
"This promise of enlargement is helping to bring Europe together. And it is a promise that must be kept," she told the NATO allies on Tuesday, appealing for a united front.
"We recognise that Russian leaders oppose the enlargement of our alliance and that this is not likely to change. But neither will we change."
Several members of the former Soviet bloc -- widely expected to be Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- will be invited at a Madrid summit in July to join NATO.
Negotiations should be completed quickly, Albright said, so that the new members could join by 1999.

A new partnership with Moscow, including the possibility of a joint NATO-Russian brigade to reinforce military cooperation, would be forged to show Russia that it had nothing to fear and could boost European security for all.

But the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), founded in 1949 to stave off the Soviet military threat, has already made clear it will not allow Russia to have any say in who joins the alliance or when.
Russia has argued that NATO enlargement will threaten its security and possibly political stability, with ailing Russian President Boris Yeltsin under heavy fire from critics at home.

Germany's Kinkel met Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Wednesday. Like others before him, he ran into a wall of opposition from the Russian political elite.
"Everyone I have met has shown resistance to NATO enlargement," Kinkel said after the talks. "We have to find a solution which allows us to have a successful summit in Madrid for all of us."
Rodionov said Kinkel had brought no new ideas.
"We are concerned that NATO...coming close to the Russian borders, will try to dictate to us its political, economic and other conditions," he told Interfax news agency.
Yeltsin, still recovering from pneumonia, reiterated demands for a legally-binding document setting out relations with NATO during a 15-minute telephone talk with Kinkel.

The Kremlin chief also repeated a demand that Russia should be admitted to the Group of Seven, the most elite group of world powers which brings together the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Canada, Britain, and Italy.

After visits from Albright and Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini this week, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is due for talks in Brussels this weekend with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.
The biggest problem in European security also tops the agenda at a U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki next month.

Solana is trying to negotiate the terms of a new NATO-Russia charter, which will provide some form of permanent consultation forum on security issues. It is the centrepiece of the alliance's efforts to reassure Russia.
Diplomats said Albright's firm insistence on a fast-track timetable to complete enlargement negotiations would not please Russia, nor make Solana's difficult job any easier.
In contrast, the foreign ministers of Poland and Hungary welcomed Albright's robust line on enlargement.

"Our satisfaction stems from the fact that...the offer to Russia does not contain clauses or propositions which would in any way limit the status of our future NATO membership and will not be a formula allowing a delay...." Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told a news conference.

Russia has carefully exploited any hint of Western differences or nervousness over enlargement, including a row over whether to hold a "big power" summit with Moscow that would exclude many NATO allies.
Albright, in appealing for a united and firm front in Brussels, underlined that this must not be allowed to deflect the alliance.
But diplomats said her suggestion of a joint NATO-Russia military unit took some allies by surprise. No details have been worked out and Moscow declined comment on the idea.

As part of its efforts to reassure Moscow, NATO has agreed to adapt a Cold War-era European arms treaty limiting conventional forces. Russia says the treaty is outdated and puts it at a huge military disadvantage.
The alliance was expected to approve formal proposals on this later on Wednesday and they would then be tabled at European security talks in Vienna on Thursday.
